speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 21, consideration in committee of Bill No. 85, to amend the Foreign Exchange Control Act- Mr. Abbott-Mr. Golding in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Kidd) asked for some information about one C. A. Rowe, an employee of the foreign exchange control board. I have that information now and I should like to give it to him.
Mr. Rowe was born in Durham, Ontario in 1913. He attended the university of Western Ontario from 1931 to 1935 and Osgoode Hall from 1935 to 1938. He was called to the bar
Foreign Exchange Control and practised law in Ontario until joining the army in 1944. Upon his discharge he joined the staff of the wartime prices and trade board in Ottawa, on October 31, 1946. On June 1, 1947, he was taken on the staff of the Bank of Canada and assigned to the enforcement section of the foreign exchange control board, where he dealt with seizures made under the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Control Act and general enforcement matters under the supervision and direction of senior officers of the board. On September 1, 1948, Mr. Rowe was transferred to the office of the board at Windsor, Ontario, where he has remained since that time.
Speaking generally, I believe that Mr. Rowe is a relatively junior employee of the board.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Am I correct in my understanding that the difference between the cost of purchasing, let us say United States currency, and sales from time to time of United States currency, is a charge on the consolidated revenue fund; or is it taken from some special fund that is at the minister's disposal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
I understand the foreign
exchange control board charges a commission when it sells United States funds, and receives a similar commission when it buys them. That is the margin of profit, if I may so describe it, which is intended to cover the operating expenses of the board. Of course if there were an exchange loss it might wipe out that profit. Is that the hon. member's question?

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: No; I did not have operating expenses in mind. I mean actual money used to purchase foreign exchange. The minister has referred from time to time to the building up of our foreign exchange reserves. That could only come out of the consolidated revenue fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: That is correct. The foreign exchange control board acts as the agent of the Minister of Finance, and the foreign exchange account is provided with money furnished by the Minister of Finance as Receiver General for Canada out of the consolidated revenue fund.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
The minister answered a question on February 28 in which I asked for the amount expended for the purchase of gold, United States currency and other foreign currencies since the enactment of the Foreign Exchange Control Act. The answer was given in the form of figures showing net purchases and net sales for each year, the net purchases indicated by a plus sign and the net sales by a minus sign. On setting the figures up and taking a rough total, one finds that the excess

Foreign Exchange Control of plus over minus under the three headings, namely purchase of gold, purchase of United States dollars, and purchase of other foreign currencies, is $981 million over a nine-year period. I should like to know if I am correct in assuming that the payments for the operation of foreign exchange control resulted in a charge upon the taxpayers of Canada of $981 million for the past nine years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: I do not know that I would put it just that way. The result of course is that while the government of Canada has advanced to the foreign exchange control board or the foreign exchange account an amount such as the hon. member suggests, there is an asset there for the corresponding liability. It is included in our account as an active asset of the government.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Presumably if control were to end tomorrow it would be represented by an amount in the consolidated revenue fund, so that perhaps we could operate without taxation for a year. But since the government has only two sources of obtaining funds, namely, taxation and borrowing, to finance the operations so far $981 million has been raised by taxes from the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Or by borrowing.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: No; it could be raised by borrowing.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: By taxation or borrowing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: If the hon. member is correct in saying that there is an apparent cost of $981 million incurred by the foreign exchange control board, how much is the active asset carried against that cost? What was the profit when the foreign exchange control board took over all the gold holdings of the banks of Canada, and perhaps any private holdings as well? I think the take-over price was at the old rate of $20 an ounce, and then it was revalued upward. The board would have a fortuitous profit there at the expense of the banks and the holders of gold in Canada. course realized some years ago. The assets the foreign exchange control board holds against the liabilities to which the hon. member for Kamloops referred are those holdings of gold and foreign currencies, principally United State currency; and they are shown in the annual report of the foreign exchange control board which I tabled a few days ago.

speechtext:
I should like to ask a question with respect to section 35 (1) (e) of the Foreign Exchange Control Act, which reads:
35(1) The governor in council may make regulations . . .
(e) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained elsewhere in this act, exempting any person or any class of persons or any transaction or class of transactions from any provision of this act.
As I read it, this provision gives the governor in council the right in certain cases to overrule this act passed by parliament. Have any regulations been made under paragraph (e) exempting any person or any class of persons or any transaction or class of transactions from any provision of the act?

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Yes, there have been; and I should be glad to give my hon. friend an enumeration of those exemptions. Most of them relate to exemptions from various permit requirements of transactions between Canada and Newfoundland. Exemption from permit regulations has been provided under section 35 (1) of the act concerning the change of address of the owner of a bank account from Canada elsewhere.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: The minister is dealing with section 35?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: Yes, section 35 (1) (e), which provides for regulations exempting persons or transactions from the provisions of the act. The cases in which this power is exercised under the regulations are, first, exemptions from various permit requirements of transactions between Canada and Newfoundland- I have a long list of them here. maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951

speechtext:
I should like to ask a question respecting section 36 of the act. The pertinent part reads:
36(1) Subject to the provisions of this act and the regulations and under the control and direction of the minister, the board may . . .
(b) In particular cases or classes of cases, from time to time prescribed terms and conditions for permits additional to those prescribed by regulation or prescribed special forms of permits in cases where none is prescribed by regulation.
As I read that section it gives the board the power to make regulations that would override regulations made by the governor in council. It gives the board the right in particular cases to amend or add to regulations, and apparently the regulations that the board makes do not have to be published in the Canada Gazette as do those made by the governor in council under section 35. In what particular cases or classes of cases has this section been acted upon?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Here again this is a provision inserted to give a reasonable degree of prac-
1750	HOUSE OF
Foreign Exchange Control tical flexibility to the act, and the variations from the formal regulations are somewhat minor in character. Section 36, subsection 1(b), as my hon. friend has pointed out, authorizes the board to prescribe special forms of permits and terms and conditions of permits additional to those contained in the regulations. Under this provision, for example, special forms of permits have been introduced for the export of currency by travelers; these are issued in lieu of the normal permit on form H.
First, there is the special border permit issued to commuters and others having occasion to cross the border frequently, authorizing them to carry a specified amount on any one trip. The permit is exhibited to a customs officer on each trip but need not be surrendered. Then there is the special business travel permit which is issued to business firms whose employees frequently require to travel to the United States on short notice when banks may be closed.
Special terms and conditions are attached to permits in various circumstances, examples of which are as follows:	First, foreign
exchange is made available for any reasonable amount for genuine business travel. Businessmen obviously cannot, in many cases, estimate in advance what expenditures they will have to make, and where large amounts are asked for, they are normally made available on condition that on his return the traveler will furnish a statement of his expenditures so that the board can satisfy itself that they were in fact for business purposes.
Second, in certain cases of capital transfers from residents to nonresidents, payment is approved on condition that the nonresident reinvest the amount in certain classes of Canadian domestic securities. The effect is that the nonresident, while retaining his investment in Canada, is able to change its character if he wishes to do so. This procedure is applied principally in the case of capital payments between related parties.
Third, where a resident is authorized to make a new capital investment abroad to establish a business, it is normally made a condition of providing exchange for that purpose that earnings from the investment will be brought back to Canada.
I think these are fairly typical examples of the latitude given under that section to the administrative body to vary the formal conditions of the general applications which are set out in the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend raised that question, because last evening I was not thoroughly familiar with the procedural steps which could be taken under the act. I have had it looked into, and here is the position. The only case in which the board can make a decision as to forfeiture is the case involving $100 or less. The procedure is provided in sections 61 and 62 of the act. Briefly it is that when the seizure is made the board notifies the owner of the reasons therefor, and calls on him to furnish within thirty days evidence relating to the seizure if he wishes to do so. If evidence is furnished it is considered by the board, and the owner is notified whether or not the seizure is to be maintained. The owner may, within thirty days thereafter, object to a decision to forfeit the funds, in which case the board is required, upon request of the owner, to refer the matter to a court. Does that answer my hon. friend's question?

The provisions of sections 61 and 62 are applicable only when there is a large amount in dispute. A person who has $20, $40 or $60 taken from him, irrespective of how unjust the circumstances may be, is in effect denied any recourse. I mentioned two cases last evening. I have at least another half dozen cases in which individuals, and properly so, resent the orders that were made. In effect they have no recourse. If they decide to go to court under the provisions of sections 61 or 62, the costs are out of proportion to the benefits that will come to them. At the end of a lawsuit, even if they are successful, they will have nothing to speak of as a result of the litigation, because the legislation does not provide for their costs to the extent that it should. I am going to make a suggestion to the minister. According to the records, those who get in touch with me, and
Foreign Exchange Control through me communicate with the foreign exchange control board, are not nearly as successful as some others must be. During the last two or three years I have followed the course of not submitting cases that in my opinion are unjustifiable. With a number of them I have done nothing, because I felt that while the applicant resented having his money taken from him, in effect he had no proper cause for complaint. In the several cases I have brought to the attention of the board I have met nothing but a blank wall.

I do not want to press individual cases. I do so merely by way of illustration. A man who lives in a small town in Saskatchewan gets word on Sunday of the funeral in the United States of a close relative. Oh, yes; I have the statute here, but in effect you are appealing from the employee to the employer. In Great Britain this type of thing is bitterly criticized in a report made in 1932 when the Lord Chancellor's committee was set up on the question of the exercise of extraordinary powers by officials. One of the recommendations was that where the rights of the individual are interfered with, that individual should have his right freed from unnecessary expense in challenging or having reviewed any order that has been made.
Those who have had less than $100 taken from them are not criminals endeavouring to evade the law. I gave an instance last evening, that of a man who, on a Sunday, arrived at the boundary and did not have a form H with him. He was asked if he had any money, and he said that he had. He was then told that he must deposit it somewhere. I have the name of the official who told him that. The man who wanted to cross the border said, "Well, the banks are closed today, and I must go over the line." The officials said they would take his money and he would have his right to apply against forfeiture. These are not isolated cases; these are cases of Canadians who are law-abiding, and who are being treated unjustly. Even at this stage I ask the minister if he will not have a review made of these cases to the end that justice be done.
The figures given last night were for the little fellows. In how many cases were seizures made of over $100, and in how many of those cases were the moneys returned as a result of representations made?
There is a third question that I should like to ask the minister. Canadians are law-abiding. Some of them want to go to the United States as tourists, and they are restricted to $150. I do not think they get very far on $150. I should like to know in how many cases persons desiring to spend the winter in another country have had special regulations made to the end that they may be provided 
with the necessary funds. Matters such as these arouse resentment and ill-feeling, and when coupled with obvious injustice in cases such as those to which I have referred, there is not only resentment against the government; there is resentment against parliament for permitting individuals to enjoy power almost unchallengeable by Canadians as a whole.

As I say, speaking generally the board has endeavoured to follow a liberal policy with respect to health applications. I notice the hon. member for Eglinton shakes his head, and I have had some experiences myself in which it seemed to me they should have accepted the medical certificates. However, generally speaking that is the case.
While I am on my feet I think I should answer the hon. member for Saint John-Albert as to the export of capital by those who may wish to sell their property and move to the United States. Section 36, subsections 1 and 2, authorize the board to determine residential status for the purposes of the act, and that power is exercised principally in dealing with applications for change of status from resident to nonresident, made by persons who wish to move from Canada and take up permanent residence elsewhere. Where the move is to a United States dollar area country the emigrant is authorized to transfer a maximum of $12,500 during the first year, in Canadian dollars, through the unofficial market. Regulations have been issued with respect to that; and at the end of one year from the departure from Canada, and at annual intervals thereafter, depending of course upon how long the restrictions may continue, the owner may apply to the board for authority to make additional transfers from Canada from these resident assets. One addition I might make to that is that a United States citizen who has been resident in Canada and who desires to return to the United States to live is normally authorized to transfer his assets to the United States at the time of departure, provided that the excess over the amount authorized for transfer in Canadian dollars is invested in Canadian domestic securities having a term of maturity or authorized call date of not less than three years.

I do not think this is the place to discuss the merits or demerits of so-called barter transactions. There is no foreign exchange control aspect involved in any case. It is true that the Foreign Exchange Control Act requires that any goods exported from this country must be payable in currency approved by the board. To that extent you cannot enter into barter transactions without permission of the board. The primary question whether a transaction of that kind should be entered into I shall not discuss at this time. My views are well known. I voiced them the other night. I believe that kind of transaction we should enter into only as a last resort.
As to the first question, with reference to acceptance of sterling as payment for exports, as indicated in the report of the board, there is no objection to that now, provided that the exporter is willing to accept that sterling and to wait until the Bank of England or the United States treasury is prepared to convert it into dollars. But if the foreign exchange control board were to take sterling from the

Canadian exporter, actually we would be simply extending further credits to the sterling area, and in addition to the credit risk we would also be incurring an exchange risk.
As I say, there is no objection; I think the board will now permit such transactions. If for instance any exporter of salmon, lumber or some other commodity is prepared to sell it and to take sterling for it, that is permitted -provided that his workmen get the necessary Canadian dollars. But the dominion government does not feel it can extend its foreign credit program by accumulating sterling.

I am afraid my hon. friend has not read carefully the prepared statements I have issued in the last two or three months in connection with the comptroller of the treasury's monthly statements, where I have been endeavouring to demonstrate the difference in public accounts between what is referred to as budgetary surplus and cash surplus. In public finance there are many items which are not budgetary items but which have to be paid for in cash. On the other side there are a great many budgetary expenditures which do not have to be made in cash. If my hon. friend will look back at my budget speech of 1947 he will find that I referred in specific terms to the fact that during the then fiscal year we had received several hundred million dollars as a result of payments made to me in my official capacity from the exchange fund account. The trend has been reversed this year; in fact we have had to provide out of the cash resources of the government between $400 million and $450 million for the exchange fund account in order to provide dollars, mainly for exporters who have turned over their United States dollars to the exchange fund account.
That fact has nothing to do with the amount of the budgetary surplus which the government has at the end of its fiscal year. It has a significant bearing on the cash requirements of the government, which is something completely different. I am not revealing any budget secrets when I say that in the course of my economic survey this evening I shall have something to say on this particular subject. Perhaps my hon. friend will accept this short explanation this morning, and this evening I hope to be able to deal with the question he has raised, which is an important one, in considerably more detail.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the comments that have been made as to the section that is now before the house indicate the necessity of recognizing exactly what the effect of the section is. On second reading the principle involved was simply whether or not foreign exchange control should be extended. That has been discussed; and naturally it is a subject which would embrace a very wide field.
The device that is being used to extend the life of this act is to carry forward an act of seventy-three sections by the adoption of a single section. It would be utterly impossible to discuss effectively at any point in the proceedings the consequences of this act, unless it were done in committee, because this section carries forward in detail the whole seventy-three sections of the act.
There is one feature of this amending section which is of basic importance and which should be given consideration in the light of remarks that have already been made both in and out of the house. The amendment to section 73 of the act proposed by the bill now before the house extends the life of the act for two years. I submit that under no circumstances should this measure be carried forward beyond one year under the present bill amendment, because when parliament meets in 1950 it can then deal with the question whether the act should be extended for another year.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext: It might take us that long to get this through.

maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL ACT
subtopic: CONTINUANCE IN FORCE UNTIL SIXTY DAYS AFTER OPENING OF FIRST SESSION OF PARLIAMENT IN 1951
speechtext:
Under the system of government that we have adopted in Canada the basic principle that has been accepted for hundreds of years is that, in relation to financial matters, there shall be an annual review by parliament, and that the authorization shall only proceed for a period of a year subject


to that review. It is questionable if there is sufficient recognition of the fundamental importance of the act which will be carried forward in toto by the amendment if it is adopted in its present form. No single act could possibly have a wider impact upon the future economic life of the country than one which can so definitely and powerfully influence the future trading relationships of Canada with all nations with which Canada deals.
To a greater extent than any other nation, with the possible exception of Switzerland, we in Canada are dependent upon the maintenance of a very large export business for continuing the standards of living which have been established in this country at a very high level. The Foreign Exchange Control Act, through its effect on exchange, which has such a bearing on trade in itself, and through its direct effect on trade under the import and export sections, can determine the whole level of trade carried on by this country in the years ahead. Therefore the act is one of immense importance to the future of Canada, and should be so regarded by those who are making a decision both as to its contents and its duration.
As the records show, an effort was made to limit the life of the act when it first came before the house. The efforts to impose such a limitation were defeated by the government and its supporters, but in the other place a limitation of three years was placed upon the life of the act. That at least was a limitation which has brought it back to the house for further consideration. In the ordinary course of events this act will not again be subject to review until after two years, no matter what disastrous consequences may ensue.
As the Minister of Finance has very properly pointed out, there is available information as to the details of the operation of the act, and the minister, under very heavy pressure in relation to other impending events, has unquestionably done everything possible to answer the detailed questions which have been put forward. But only information will be received; and while it is true that it is open to parliament at any session to repeal the act, the fact remains that under ordinary circumstances the act as it now stands would carry forward for two years, thus placing ordinary discussion of the operation of the act beyond the control of parliament for the whole of that period. That is undoubtedly something which should be regarded in the light not only of the general principle involved, but also of statements made by those who should be in a better position than anyone else in the house to know what the circumstances actually are or to advise hon. members.

As it stands at the moment, in view of the enormous and, may I add, humanitarian considerations which have guided the course of the United States in dealing with Marshall aid and the financial assistance of European and other countries, undoubtedly those charged with the responsibility of administration of those funds have more expert knowledge available to them than anyone else who could discuss the subject. For that reason it is of importance in considering this matter to recognize what has been said by Mr. Hoffman, administrator of the ECA, and the man charged with the major responsibility of allocating Marshall plan payments. Mr. Hoffman has said unqualifiedly that there must be stabilization of currency in 1949. If that is the view of Mr. Hoffman, the man more responsible than anyone else, outside the government of the United States, for what will be done either through the international monetary fund or through any other agency of the United States government or of the United Nations, it seems to me the parliament of Canada should not be prepared to extend the life of this foreign exchange control bill, which is also a control over export and import, beyond the period of one year. It is within the power of the government to deal with that matter by indicating its willingness to limit the life of this measure to one year, but that must be done while we are in committee if it is to be done at all, unless the bill is referred back from third reading for further consideration by this committee. I would strongly urge the Minister of Finance to recognize the basic principle involved in the continuation of this bill of seventy-three sections, and also to observe the explicit statement by Mr. Hoffman that there must be currency stabilization in 1949.
When it comes to the question of dealing with our own exchange rate, a great deal has been said about the use of the word "realistic" in relation to the actual value of Canadian money. So far as that is concerned, the word "realistic" has been widely used by the official advisers to this government; and one statement that has been made, which it seems to me should commend itself to hon. members of this house, is that fixed exchange rates have lost touch with economic realities. We are not the inventors of the word "realistic" or the words "economic realities." What the Minister of Agriculture has said is exactly what has been put forward by the members of the Progressive Conservative party. Since Canada has very properly asserted its increasing importance in the world, there is no reason why Canada should wait for any other country, and there is a special reason why Canada should be the first nation to insist upon a realistic review of the whole situation and attempt, with the assistance of the best brains available in the western world, to find some way of restoring the convertibility factor between the pound and the dollar.

Foreign Exchange Control international monetary fund. Unless a solution of this problem of interchangeability is found, this country may well be heading for disaster.	.
The Minister of Agriculture has indicated quite clearly the dangers to the export of our commodities under the rigidity which now exists. Sir Stafford Cripps has given us an ominous warning of what may happen if we do not find some way of restoring interchangeability. Mr. Hoffman has made it clear that the solution must be found this year. Therefore I urge the government without delay to press for an immediate meeting of the governments and their experts to explore the possibility of restoring interchangeability of these funds and of laying the foundation for the kind of trade that this country through a realistic exchange really can have for its people to meet the demands of a hungry world.
In accordance with our general practice, this act should be limited to one year. Mr. Hoffman has said that the solution must be found this year. For these reasons, among others, we shall vote against the bill. No matter how determined the government may be to carry this measure forward in its present form, I urge that this extension be limited to a period of one year, so that there may be some compulsion and within the year a solution may be found which will open the channels of trade for Canada to the whole world.

In dealing with the effect of the adoption of this bill at this time, I do not believe it would be possible to put the situation which results from a decision to adopt an omnibus measure of this nature into more accurate terms than can be found in the words of the right hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he spoke in this house on April 1, 1932, when the government of that day sought certain powers under the general reference to peace, order and good government, the reference under which the present steps must be taken if they are to be taken at all. The words I now read are taken from his speech on that occasion, with certain omissions from the total of the speech:
Peace, order and good government include virtually everything. . . . That no doubt is the kind of thing the Prime Minister would like to bring about; to establish himself as a dictator, as a second Cromwell in his day, but I say that, before we

return to the days of the revolution, we shall do our utmost to prevent a reversion to any condition such as that.
Let me ask my hon. friend . . . how would he feel if a socialist government were in office at the present time and, under the rights claimed by the ministry of which he is a member, attempted to legislate with respect to peace, order and good government, and to deal with the very subjects with which he and his colleagues have dealt? How would he feel if they passed an order in council to amend the Bank Act without any reference to parliament? How would he feel if they said that, by virtue of a situation which had arisen, the banks of the country should no longer be permitted to carry on their business under the provisions of the act which parliament had enacted; that it was necessary to amend that act, and then proceeded, by order in council, to amend the Bank Act? . . .
Let us consider the question of the insurance companies. How would my hon. friend view the action of a socialist ministry which said; We do not care what the law is with respect to insurance companies, we are going to pass by order in council the legislation which we think is necessary in this time of crisis to make these insurance companies do whatever we believe to be in the interests of the country. . . .
That is the position in which we are at the present time. May I go a step further? . . . How would my Conservative friends feel if a socialist government in office, using the precedent of the action taken by the present ministry under authority to legislate on peace, order and good government, started forthwith to have the printing presses of this country manufacture whatever money they wished and to distribute that money broadcast, giving as a reason that this was necessary in order to meet a situation which existed? . . .
I hear an hon. member opposite say that there will be no socialist government. May I say to him that this is the kind of thing that breeds socialist governments of the most extreme type. This is the sort of thing that would provide any government with the weapons it might need in order, if it so desired, to deal in a subversive manner with the constitution and other rights of the people. . . .
I am endeavouring to place before hon. gentlemen the position as it would present itself to them if a socialist government attempted to do what they themselves are doing. I do not believe that any government, socialist or otherwise, except this one would attempt to go the autocratic lengths that hon. gentlemen opposite have gone, but I do say that any government would find ample justification in .he form of precedent for any extreme act, in the action of hon. gentlemen opposite in this particular measure which gives to the government of the day the authority which it does. That is the point I wish to make.
We all know very well that extreme action of the kind for which hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible does not come about in a day. Arbitrary authority helps to breed arbitrary authority. The enjoyment of a ce"tain amount of absolute power creates an appetite for more in the way of absolute power, and finally absolutism knows no bounds. That is the point we have now reached so far as the Prime Minister and his colleagues are concerned.
Those words of the right hon. member for Glengarry are in every respect applicable to the measure now before this house, except for the fact that it confers infinitely wider powers than were ever dreamed of in the bill under discussion at the time these statements were made.

Those words of the right hon. member for Glengarry were directed to a very limited field of the exercise of the emergency powers. They were limited to a specific measure. Before us now we have an omnibus measure which is the continuance of the application of extended powers; and the fact that these have been reduced to twelve in number in no way changes the principle which is inherent in the contention that this house should pass this omnibus measure covering all these wartime orders in council.
We are not asked as a House of Commons to consider a rent control bill. We are not asked to consider a price control bill. The only bill that the members of this house are asked to consider is a bill which gives to this government all the loose and undefined powers of a dictatorship over the whole timber industry, the whole steel industry, over all industrial and other building priorities, and several other extremely important activities of our people, as well as unsatisfactory and undefined authority over rent and prices. Whether they are tenants or not, Canadians generally know that the present rent control by government dictate, and not by law, has proved unsatisfactory in many important respects, quite apart from the dangerous principle involved in these arbitrary powers, which include the whole field under the declaration of a general emergency.
In many ways this rent control measure by government dictate is adding to the difficulties and preventing the building of satisfactory rental housing. We have urged over and over again that a rent control bill be introduced which will give tenants defined and assured legal rights and at the same time encourage the building of housing and apartments for rental purposes. That is the parliamentary way to deal with this subject. It is
1768	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act the parliamentary way to deal with price control. It is the parliamentary way to deal with any other matter covered by this omnibus bill perpetuating wartime emergency orders in council which give to bureaucrats who are not answerable to parliament, and some who are, dictatorial powers over a large segment of our domestic economy.
When it is suggested that it is necessary to follow this arbitrary procedure in order to continue these other measures, that contention is simply unadulterated nonsense. There is no reason why a bill cannot be brought in separately to deal with any of these subjects. The same justification which would give the power to deal with the broad field would more than give power to deal with the specific field where an emergency is shown in that respect. This measure simply puts before us the continuance of powers that were put into effect in wartime, when everybody was under the pressure of war itself. Today there is no excuse for continuing measures of that kind. At the time that these arbitrary measures were first adopted, many unselfish citizens of this country were, at considerable sacrifice of their personal time, acting in the role of controllers or supervisors of some of these arbitrary measures. Those men are no longer available. Now the people who are directing these affairs are mostly civil servants-excellent civil servants-who should have the protection of dealing with the problems placed before them under clearly defined laws, not dictates of this government.
I did not of course hear the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gar son) last night. I must say that that was a saving of time. But nevertheless I do know something of what he said. When the Minister of Justice demonstrates the profound depths of his historic knowledge by referring to me as the Bay street Hampden, thus emulating his leader in the house, I do hope that he will not get into difficulties with his sponsors, the Siftons. I hope he will remember that those legatees of the great political beneficence of an earlier Liberal government have established the head office of the corporation which handles their great inherited wealth on the same Bay street in Toronto to which the Minister of Justice refers with such scorn. The Siftons might not like his attitude toward the street from which they have chosen to direct their great interests in western Canada.
When the Minister of Justice seeks to defend in this manner the conduct of a government so rapidly approaching parliamentary and physical dissolution, the description


which fits him most perfectly is to be found in the familiar words, slightly modified:
The boy stood on the burning deck,
Whence all with sense had fled.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on second reading of this bill, the issue is whether war emergency powers continue, and whether a general emergency exists, which gives to our constitution at the present time no continuing sanctity except the whims of this dictatorial government.

Mr. Chairman, there are certain matters that can be better discussed in committee than on second reading. I should like to deal with a number of these matters which were referred to last evening by the Minister of Justice. However, at the beginning I wish to reiterate the stand taken by this party, a stand which was made most clear in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton, which had just been ruled out of order. While respecting the ruling of the chair, in order to keep the record clear I should like to refer to the wording of that amendment. It reads:
That the said bill be not now read the second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I never saw so many Speakers in the house before. Hon. members apparently do not believe that the person occupying the chair can make rulings without their assistance. The amendment continued:
-with instructions that they have power to recommend a specific measure relating to rent control, and other specific measures relating respectively to other matters provided for in the said bill.
The amendment sets forth the stand taken by the opposition. We believe in the necessity for certain controls while at the same time accepting the necessity for decontrol as referred to by the Minister of Justice. We on this side of the house asked that the bill be referred to a committee so that evidence could be heard. It would be interesting to hear the evidence of some of these individuals occupying bureaucratic positions were they required to come before a committee and outline their ideas, which apparently have actuated the government all through the piece. We say that we require evidence on this matter.
That there was doubt in the minds of the cabinet on this legislation is perfectly clear from what the chairman of the transitional powers committee of the cabinet said on November 24 last. He, the Solicitor General, at a press conference, said among other things:
Possibly the last use of procedure by order in council under Canada's emergency transitional powers act has been made by the federal cabinet.
Apparently that was before the Minister of Justice achieved his portfolio. At that time the Solicitor General was speaking for the Department of Justice. The report continued:
Mr. Jean said he is due to present in Ottawa tomorrow his final report as head of a committee on application of the emergency powers.

The report having been referred to at a press conference, I think parliament should be let in on it. The Minister of Justice should present to parliament the report to which the Solicitor General made reference. The Solicitor General went on to say that he hoped there would be no further necessity for cabinet orders under the legislation designed to ease the country from war to a peacetime administrative footing. The minister should explain when the transition -not under the transitional powers act- took place in the minds of the cabinet. At what time since November 24 did the cabinet decide not to follow the recommendations of the chairman of the committee set up by the cabinet to consider this matter? That is an interesting document that should be before parliament when it is arriving at a conclusion respecting the existence of a general emergency.
The minister said last evening, as reported on page 1729 of Hansard:
Our powers are very narrowly limited and any suggestion about widespread totalitarian dictatorial powers which flout parliament is just so much nonsense.
He asked whether anyone could produce proof to the contrary. A case that I produce is one decided in 1948 in the exchequer court, Belleau versus Minister of National Health and Welfare. I shall not go into the details, but here is what was said by one of the protectors of the rights of the people in this country, namely, a member of the judiciary. The minister, speaking partly I believe as a politician and not exclusively as the custodian of justice in this country, said that there were no serious encroachments on personal rights, but this is what the judge said:
The court has no power under the law to prevent a minister from transgressing his administrative function and entering into the judicial field.
Mark these words.
There are, in my judgment, far too many encroachments by ministers, deputy ministers and functionaries in the judicial as well as in the legislative field;
Last night the minister said that there was no such danger as the leader of the opposition feared from this legislation, namely, the incipient beginning of a dictatorship, but a judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada, referring to ministers, deputy ministers and such functionaries, said this in his judgment: -if they are not curtailed the country may in a not too remote future be ruled by a dictatorial government.
I ask the Minister of Justice whether the opinion of a judge of the Exchequer Court of Canada has not a meaning which the words of a minister would not have. The judge decided that the minister had done wrong

and was unjustified in what he had done, in that he had entrusted his administration with wide and exorbitant powers, and concluded his judgment:
I have no other alternative but to accept reluctantly I must say the doctrine expounded on behalf of respondents.
In other words, however dictatorial and unjust an order made by a minister under legislation alike and akin to this legislation, or by a deputy minister or a functionary, the decision would be above the courts and could not be interfered with in any way.

I do not know where to begin in the quoting of editorials referring to powers such as are asked for under this legislation for the period of one more year. I am sure if I quoted the Globe and Mail it would meet with immediate support from the other side, but I am not going to do that. I am going to quote from the Winnipeg Free Press, which the minister must accept as an authority, and the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix, which has never been noted for its support of the opposition. As far as the Winnipeg Free Press is concerned, it has this to say:
It is easy to say that Canadian liberty is perfectly safe in the hands of the present government. The record shows it is not safe in the hands of the present government.
Yet we are asked to place these powers, and I refer to those with the exception of

Transitional Measures Act the matter of rent control and any other controls that may be necessary, in the hands of a government that has shown a psychopathic contempt for parliament, and has placed itself above the law in orders in council passed under the powers conferred by this act. It is unhappily true that the present Liberal administration, while it has devised and executed broad fiscal, trading and security policies . . . has failed miserably these past few years in keeping clean and free those points where policies impinge on the individual citizen, and on his rights and responsibilities as a citizen. So as Liberals meet to choose their candidates let them make their voices heard.
I point out that this quotation is not from a Progressive Conservative paper, but from a paper which at all times has given real support to the government of my hon. friend in the province of Manitoba, while he was premier and before.
Let them-

-not deny that they resent and denounce government by order in council;

I have been most restrained in my language. Instead of making statements myself I am adopting the words of organs that in the past have given the strongest support to the government, and I have been pointing out what will follow from legislation such as this. Last evening my hon. friend, the Minister of Justice, in the absence of the leader of the opposition made a very strong attack on him. The essence of that attack was that freedom was safe in the

hands of the government under this legislation by delegation whereas the experience of the last three years has shown that whenever the opportunity has arisen for this government to evade the responsibility of parliament it has done so under this legislation. I ask the right to read what is said in this newspaper editorial in regard to the exercise of these powers, because it represents exactly the criticism of the leader of the opposition as well as the criticism offered by the right hon. member for Glengarry on April 1, 1932, which was just quoted by the leader of the opposition. This editorial points out:
Let them not deny that they resent and denounce government by order in council; that they condemn the delegation of cabinet power and responsibility to boards, commissions and crown corporations elevated to a world where parliamentary interference is resented and beyond the control of our tested political system.
Can anything be stronger than that-that this government, under legislation such as this, has elevated bureaucrats in this country to a position where they have power to push individual Canadians about, without permitting those Canadians recourse to the courts? And they are asking for this power for one more year, though in November last the Solicitor General said in effect: "We are at the end of the road, as far as I can see, in connection with this legislation." Then the editorial goes on:
Let them as Liberals make it clear that they will no longer passively accept the interpretation of our laws by non-responsible officials and the progressive weakening of our judicial system to which alone we can safely entrust this function of government...
Let them reject and outlaw the political considerations which have led to state appointments which will scarcely enrich our public institutions. Let them refuse to accept or countenance interference in their deliberations by those of their leaders who are infected with the disease of machinism.
I shall let hon. gentlemen on the front benches determine which of the leaders are infected with the disease of machinism. We of the opposition have consistently followed the course-and I have the quotations over the years-that where there is necessity for individual controls because of scarcity or by reason of economic conditions, we accept them. But we demand that the government, while holding out as bait the bringing into effect of necessary controls, shall not at the same time bring in controls that are not necessary, in order to perpetuate and preserve the bureaucracy that has been rampant in this country during the last two or three years. That is the stand taken by the opposition. I could give quotation after quotation from Liberal newspapers in this country calling upon parliament to cease its passivity, and calling upon members supporting the government to forget that one of the major offences they can commit is to stand against

a decision of the government front benches; asking them to stand up in this house, as members representative of the people, against an oppression that is arising by reason of bureaucratic control above and beyond the reach of the courts.
You asked me, Mr. Chairman, not to refer to the 1945 act. I shall not do so, except to say that this is a continuation-

Any representations either in favour of extending it to 1950 or against extending it for the full year are in order, or any question about changing the date; but a general discussion of the principle of extension which was approved on second reading would not be in order at this time.
