speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I find it difficult to know what it would be possible to discuss on an occasion like this, if it were not the degree to which the powers that are being granted will be utilized in the period between now and March 31, 1950. I realize your fairness at all times, Mr. Chairman, and I do not want to do anything that would constitute even the slightest departure from your ruling, so I shall not press the point further. I realize that this is one subject my hon. friends opposite do not want discussed.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Don't take yourself too seriously.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: As far as my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce is concerned the abuse of power is one subject which always arouses him. He is a Chesterfield of parliamentary manners until there is any reference to the way in which he and those associated with him have flouted parliament. Then he immediately becomes aroused and resorts to his usual attitude, which he is now displaying. I expect a higher degree of intelligence from my right hon. friend than he displayed in the interjection he just made. I can understand his attitude, however, for he is the man who was responsible for the order in council which denied to parliament-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I raise a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Surely this is not in order.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I suggest that the hon. gentleman be allowed to proceed, for I should like to reply to him with the same latitude.
Transitional Measures Act

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The right hon. minister made his point, and I have allowed the hon. member for Lake Centre to reply, so I believe he should return to the bill.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Another waste of time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend has some remark to make?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Get back to the bill.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Let me tell my hon. friend that ignorance, even though energetic, is still ignorance.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: A waste of time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is difficult to continue against all this noise, Mr. Chairman. The area in the back is now engaged in general disorder. However, I want to ascertain from the minister the degree to which, when these powers are granted, the individual who is affected will have the right of recourse to the courts against injustice and unfairness. I think it only fair that there be an assurance in that direction. The principle has been decided by the house already, that there is to be an extension of powers for a further year; and as custodian of the rights of the people in this country I think the Minister of Justice should give the assurance now and place the necessary amendment in this legislation so that no longer will orders in council be passed by the Star Chamber method and kept in secret for several months, to be produced ultimately only when some hon. member discovers their existence. Will he make provision in the act whereby any person wrongly interfered with or unjustly treated or in any way discriminated against in his own class to his own detriment will have the right of recourse to the courts? We have a right to ask that if extraordinary powers are to be granted they shall be so circumscribed that no man in this country will be denied his right of appeal to the courts against injustice caused to him as the result of a misapplication, if you will, of the powers granted under this act.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I want to point out to the attorney general one feature of this particular bill. Since confederation it has always been the rule, by maxim and tradition, that the hon. gentleman who is Attorney General of Canada must not give to the house legal opinions. The hon. gentleman has been violating that rule every day of the week. I happened to have a pair in the first vote today. I was unfortunately not here at the time Bill 86 was called, but 1 was called in. Legal opinions have been given across this chamber every five minutes, and it is a breach of the statute law. The hon. gentleman may be brought into litigation between the attorney general of the dominion and the attorneys

Transitional Measures Act general of the provinces with regard to what is a general emergency under Bill 86 and what is not. A general emergency takes precedence over everything from coast to coast in Canada, provided that it is of general application and within the terms of section 91, which makes the dominion, in case of war and general emergency, supreme over section 92 and over everything we have in this country.
I wish to point out only four or five things in conclusion. I hope we shall not have any more violations of that kind by the present attorney general. I happened to point out this rule to his predecessor, who is now the Prime Minister of Canada, during the first three or four days he was in the house. At that time a bill was under consideration as a result of which litigation might arise between the Attorney General of Canada and the attorneys general of three or four of the provinces. It was pointed out that, by a decision of the privy council, this was a rule of law in England. While the names of their ministers over there are a little bit different, the principle is the same; the attorney general must not give legal opinions in the house, even if he is asked to do so.
The other question to which I wish to refer is one that I probably should have raised on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Eglinton. I shall not go far with it today. In three or four minutes I shall conclude my remarks. At the Canadian National Exhibition grounds in Toronto on May 20 there is to be an exhibition by the Home Builders Association with regard to prefabricated housing, and I hope all hon. members will find it possible to see it. I remember mentioning this matter of housing three or four years ago when Mr. Churchill, then Prime Minister of Great Britain, was getting lumber and many other things for that type of housing. I have here in my hand a pamphlet announcing the exhibition which is to be in the horticulture building. Houses that can be built for $1,200 are to be shown.
As I said before in connection with the building of civic car lines in our city, I remember when we had a similar situation in Toronto. The old street railway went only up to Bloor street, under the old street railway agreement. Between 1915 and 1921 a system of civic car lines was built-six tickets for ten cents-one on St. Clair running right out to the junction, one in North Toronto, in Eglinton riding, by the taking over of the metropolitan railway out there, one of these civic car lines on Gerrard street from Broadview to east end, and one on Danforth from Broadview to Main street. With these municipal civic car services, with six tickets for ten cents, the whole territory was opened up and the people built their own houses.

The last thing I wish to say is this. We have no steam suburban service, as they have in Montreal and every large American city. We must have one if we are ever going to solve the housing problem. Land could be bought by the acre in the country but as long as we have no steam suburban service we are not able to obtain it. Other large cities have such a service. I believe western Ontario is suffering badly, as is the Niagara district and the Toronto district especially, from choked railway facilities without a steam suburban service. In York, Peel and Ontario counties land is cheap but without municipal services, and in the city no lands are available for that type of housing at a cost that the workingman can pay.
As I said here the other night on, I believe, another section of this particular bill, it is time that we had some provision along those lines. Speaking as a private member of the house I went so far as to say that I believe the time has come when there should be some subsidy in connection with workingmen's houses. For the low-wage people there is a fund under the Workmen's Compensation Act to which the Minister of Labour makes considerable reference. This matter could be worked out under the Workmen's Compensation Act, plus a food subsidy along the same lines, through the Workmen's Compensation Act, to meet the needs of the low paid wage earners. I remember when Mr. Churchill, the former Prime Minister of Great Britain, made an address in which he was urging the building of 500,000 prefabricated houses. We need almost that many in Canada right now. With the cheap land which can be had out in the townships, and with a steam suburban service, a solution might be found. Take, for instance, Lome Park. There is only one train a day out there. In East York there are no trains at all. The city gives services and we paid large sums of money to build roads, the York highways which I instituted in 1907, fifteen miles out.
There are various classes of housing that might be referred to today. I am afraid I come pretty close to the rule that it is not in order to discuss these matters under this bill. I might mention that there is housing for the Indians and the Eskimos. We had committees on these matters. In my constituency three or four hundred people are being housed in the old jail, which has accommodation for only 130. We managed that by building two jail farms, one for men and one for women, when I was in office, and the old Toronto jail was used only for remands. It is a question of the sick. No doubt the Ontario government needed those two farms for the mental hospitals. They

are doing excellent work in that connection and have made a great deal of improvement. But the old Toronto jail should be used only for remands and the excess given new quarters.
There is the question of housing for the aged and infirm, and there are a great many other features of the housing problem which I shall be obliged to mention at another time.
I call to your attention, however, the fact that what we need in the Toronto district is a steam suburban service. Every large city has such a service. Without it there can be no solution to the housing problem, because that problem is almost ninety per cent a transportation problem plus municipal services problem. If these cannot be given at a small cost-and I hope the Minister of Labour can work it out in some way-plus some allowance for food for the workingman's family and part for cheap housing, then I do not know where we are going to be in the Toronto district, where we need such a large number of houses for the working classes.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not
suppose there is much possibility that all members of this house will agree on this bill anyway. That would be too much to expect. The Progressive Conservative party naturally takes the attitude that we have too many controls embodied in this bill. Of course our friends of the C.C.F. party suggest that there are not nearly enough controls.
Last night I was particularly interested to hear the hon. member for Moose Jaw say that his party would not suggest that controls be continued for one moment beyond the time when prices were no longer rising. It seems to me that the attitude which they have taken recently shows their interest in retaining floor prices for most of the products which the farmers sell in Saskatchewan.
I: would suggest to the minister that he might adopt the philosophy of the Chinese. It might be helpful if he allowed all of us to save face in a matter of this kind. I suggest that one control that he could well remove is that on timber. I am not sure that he is convinced himself that he really needs the power to control timber.
In reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Victoria (Ont.) the minister said that he was interested in retaining sufficient clears in Canada to take care of the situation. I know the minister will concede immediately that there are all kinds of lumber available in Canada for building houses. If it is merely a question of controlling clears to take care of our flooring needs, I wonder whether it would not be wiser to let the individual buyer decide for himself what
Transitional Measures Act price should be paid for clear flooring. He may decide that he would like to put down shiplap flooring or something of that quality, and then cover it with wall carpet. It seems to me that each of us should be able to make the decision for himself. The price could very well be determined between the buyer and the seller, and there would be no hardship because there is always an alternative.
The same thing applies to the use of clear lumber for doors and for window stock. After all, there is always an alternative available in the form of plywood, or it could even be metal. I ask the minister whether he would consider getting rid of timber control, because I am satisfied he has sufficient administrative duties without taking on this extra one.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to follow the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. As a matter of fact, he and I have talked about this on two or three different occasions. I have also had letters from quite a few lumber companies in Ontario, and I have talked to members here who are interested in lumbering or in the lumber industries in their ridings. I have also talked to men from the maritimes, Quebec and British Columbia. Since this bill controls the lumber industry from the tree to the root under the ground, and from the log to the finished product, there is no doubt in my mind that the government can do whatever they wish . about it. They have the power.
At the present time I have a carryover of lumber in my own yard, and I know that every lumberman has lumber in his yard. Pine, according to grade, is down from $5 to $20 a thousand. Spruce is down on the average $10 a thousand. Hemlock is down on the average about $5 a thousand, and you cannot sell hardwood flooring stock at all. There is no market for it. I should like to prevail upon the minister to throw timber controls out the window, because there is no doubt that lumber for houses can be obtained, flooring, or anything else. I should be glad to have the business at twenty-five cents a thousand.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Twenty-five cents a
thousand.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, commission for supplying the government with lumber, or anybody else who wants to use it. The orders would be so big that I would make a lot more money. There is a market for hardwood in the United States, but because of the quotas we cannot fill them. The government should talk with some of the lumber concerns, and the Canadian lumbermen's association, and do something immediately. Now is the opportune time to do it because there are large cuts this

Transitional Measures Act year and some carryover from last year. Unless something is done along that line within the next few weeks the lumber industry will be left in a precarious position.
In my own riding this year there happens to be a hydro line being built which is occupying the time of 237 men from my own township. I made it my business to find out about that. If these 237 men had not been working on that hydro line, which has been cut out and is now practically finished, I do not know what we would have done with the men in Haliburton because there just would not have been any work for them to do. We had a cut of lumber taken out this year at a high cost.
I think the minister will agree that when he took certain controls off lumber in the past, when he took price control off, the lumbermen's association held the price down so that there was no increase. At any rate, there was very little, if any, increase in the price of lumber. I think he will agree also that the lumbermen are fairly reasonable fellows to deal with. He would be on safe ground in taking off these quotas and letting us ship some of this hardwood flooring to the United States.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The price has gone up.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member has not looked up the statistics. If he does that he will find that lumber has not increased in the last twelve months since controls were taken off. At the present time we do not need' timber controls at all. I have stacks of letters and telegrams which I would like to show the minister if he wishes to see them. I should like him to consider this immediately.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There must be something radically wrong with the lumber and timber business, particularly when the hon. member who has just taken his seat has told us that he could not sell flooring any more. There is a good reason for that. The reason is that the price is entirely against better sales of flooring. In my home town last fall it cost only $315 a thousand for edge-grain flooring, and for oak flooring, mill run, only $350 a thousand, and half of it was not fit to put in a floor. Perhaps some of these things are responsible for the lumbermen not being able to sell their flooring. Other materials are in the same category.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I say at once that no one would like to get rid of timber control any more than I would. My difficulty is that when the trade as a whole are consulted their opinions are different from the individual opinions expressed in this house. I sent the co-ordinator of controls out to the Pacific coast a short time ago to discuss with the trade there 
whether we could not now drop timber controls. The reply was, "please, no". They gave as the reason that they were facing negotiation of new contracts with the United Kingdom and they wanted the government in there to work out with the trade any contracts that could be arranged with the United Kingdom.
Another case in point is the situation in the maritime provinces. Last year the maritime provinces had a timber contract from the United Kingdom for 60 million feet of lumber. Recently, the United Kingdom has come in with a demand, government to government, for more than twice that amount of timber. How would we be placed if there were no control of the industry? How would we know that the larger quantity could be supplied without upsetting the local market? By working out the larger exports on a quota basis we know that the quantity can be supplied.
In addition, the United Kingdom is coming in for 10 million feet of hardwood, which is the material my hon. friend spoke about. Suppose everybody were free to ship their hardwood wherever they liked. You could not touch that business. It is all very well for hon. members to rise in their places and say that this control bothers some individual, and that he could make more money if there were no control, and therefore there must be no control. We try to look at the industry as a whole, and Canada's interest in the industry, which is very real indeed. We are trying to cut the control down to the absolute minimum. My hon. friend knows that there is no price control. The control today is solely an export control. There is no other control. We think export control is needed. We would like the industry as a whole to tell us it is not needed, and we would then get rid of it. But when we ask the industry to do so, it backs away and says, "We think we should have it". I think we should have it, too, because otherwise I think the upset in our domestic economy would be considerable, and that the effect on exports, particularly on exports to the United Kingdom, would not be beneficial.
The timber trade of the United Kingdom is under government control. That buyer comes in for very large orders which no one firm could begin to handle. Whether the industry by itself is sufficiently organized to see that those orders are taken and fairly distributed among all the producers of lumber, I am not sure. I wish they would tell me that they are so organized.
As I say, there are always two sides to this question. The hon. member has suggested that there was no increase in price when

price control went off. I would remind him that the wholesale price on lumber on the Pacific coast for the domestic market was $29 a thousand when price control was removed, and inside of a month the price level soared to about double that level.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You can buy clears on the market right now for $45.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was talking about $29, when we had price control.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How will the timber control allocate bulk purchases from the old country? If they want half a billion feet of lumber, how will the small producers in British Columbia obtain the same pro rata share of that business as the large producers? It is well known that there are several large exporting companies in British Columbia, and that they have had a number of smaller mills working for them under contract. How will those smaller mills receive their share of the business? Is it part of the business of the timber- controller to direct that?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, and I think timber control has worked to that end. If the market gets slack, or if the chief outlet is a United States market, it is much more difficult to bring that about. But for United Kingdom market orders I believe timber control has always been able to see that the order was distributed among the large and small operators.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not wish to appear persistent, but at some time in this debate I hope the Minister of Justice will tell us what the government has done about the report of the prices committee, or what it intends to do. I do not know if this is the place to do it, but some time before this debate is over I wish the minister would tell us that. What has he done about those fourteen recommendations, or what is he going to do about them -if anything?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The remarks of the minister are of considerable consequence. I took down some of them concerning control. One of his observations on timber control was that no one would be more pleased than he would to get rid of it. While these are not his exact words, he did say he had found the industry was anxious to continue controls.
That is not the basis upon which these control bills were first introduced. They were brought in on the basis of an emergency. I shall not attempt to go into that argument again, but that was the basis for their introduction. Now we reach the point where this business of timber control becomes a matter of marketing, to use the
Transitional Measures Act minister's words. He says that, looking at the industry as a whole and having regard to Canada's interests in it, the government feels that these controls should be continued for another year.
It seems to me that in respect of timber control we are now being told it is to be continued as a marketing project. We are now in the business of marketing timber. That may be a proper procedure in the ordinary course of events, but certainly it arrives at the wrong end of this matter of controls. So much for that.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I answer the point the hon. member makes? I would remind him that I said timber control today was reduced solely to export control. I would remind him further that export control is a statute of the government which does not depend upon an emergency. It depends upon permanent legislation passed by this house. The hon. member ought not to get his blood pressure too high when he discusses timber control as it is today. There is no infringement of any other jurisdiction; export control is a matter within the federal government jurisdiction.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not suggesting there is any infringement. I am simply taking the minister's reasons for having this control. If it could be done under the other measure, well and good. But why tell us that this control measure is necessary in respect of timber? Then, coming to the matter of steel-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Order. The clause before the committee deals with the extension of time.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My point is directed to that. With respect to the control on steel, I believe the data handed out by the steel industry in Canada and in the United States all goes to point out that by the third quarter of this year steel will be in good supply in this country. The minister can correct me if I am wrong, but that is the statement made by the steel industry itself.
I know that in Toronto the transportation commission, which has been waiting for many years to begin work on a big project, has now made arrangements for its steel, and is getting it from month to month. I do not know whether the steel is being produced at the present time, but the contract has been made. As I see it, the minister has no problem in steel control for the year 1949. I see no reason why it should be continued for another year. It is tied up with the export-import control regulation. Under that measure we know that all the steel coming into this country is welcome. We want all

Transitional Measures Act we can get. The controller exercises no control over it, except that it is regulated from one plant to another in order that the best interests of industry may be served. But that is a matter of internal economy. I see no reason why that cannot be taken care of under the export-import control measure.
The minister has said that this bill, in respect of the export of timber, does exercise control of the timber of the country, but only to that extent. I think this control bill is being used now more or less for the purpose of regulating trade, rather than for its original purpose of dealing with an emergency in Canada. The minister is bound at this stage to state specifically why steel control should be continued for another year.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think it would be well to let the committee know just what steel control has accomplished. I would point out to the hon. member that steel control directs the rolling schedules of the producing mills in Canada. It is all very well for the hon. member to say that we do not need steel control because in the third quarter we shall have an ample supply. I would remind him that we are still in the first quarter, and that we have to live through the second quarter.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the minister tell the committee that he believes there will be plenty of steel in the third quarter?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Certainly not; and I suggest if my hon. friend is putting that out as his expert opinion he is misleading a great many people in Canada who should be better advised. Last year we produced about 3 million tons of steel and we imported about one million tons. Of the 3 million tons that were produced in this country, 330,000 tons were produced due only to the fact that the steel controller stepped into the distribution of basic steel. Under the authority of the emergency act the steel controller took basic steel from Algoma and Dosco and shipped it to the finishing mills at Hamilton which had an additional finishing capacity. The result was the production of about 300,000 tons of steel plate that would not otherwise have been produced.
Similarly, in the matter of pig iron we said to some of the big producers: We are sorry; we shall have to have part of your pig iron; it is true you need it for your own production, but you will have to do with less. Otherwise foundries will be closed unless we get additional supplies to them that are not available from usual market sources.
In the matter of scrap steel, the controller has arranged for the importation of about 300,000 tons of scrap from Cuba, Australia and other countries. A good deal is coming 
in now from Germany and other foreign countries that would not otherwise have been available to private industry; it was made available by the government agencies directed by the steel controller. In some cases it has been necessary to subsidize the movement of scrap so that it could be used by our steel industry without upsetting the prices of the products.
A good deal was said last year about nail production. We stepped into the distribution of wire and rod suitable for being made into nails. There can be only so much nail wire and nail rod produced in this country, because our capacity is limited. We stepped in and said: We are sorry, but you cannot use as much of that nail wire and rod for wire fencing as has been your custom; we have to have a certain additional proportion of it for nails. Recently we completed a most complicated transaction in which we have had the assistance of the United States government. Certain nail wire and rod from United States mills has been allocated to Canadian mills so that this year we shall be able to produce an additional 24,000 kegs of nails per month. It will not now be necessary to interfere with our wire fencing program.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will any of those nails be exported, like those referred to a few weeks ago which were produced from wire that had been brought in?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No; that was simply a conversion process. In this case the mills have bought the wire and the product will be wholly distributed in Canada.
The steel controller is supporting certain national programs. In other words, he gives an undertaking to a manufacturer that if he takes on a program in this class which is approved by the steel controller, the steel controller will see that the necessary steel is produced. These programs include shipbuilding; freight car construction; hydroelectric expansion; railway maintenance and repair; locomotive construction; the expansion of the petroleum industry, both construction and refining; and housing construction.
Through the efforts of the steel controller and the government, the import of steel from England has been stepped up greatly. This steel has not gone into just one program; it has gone into a number of programs. The net result has been that we have been able to relieve the capacity of one of our own steel mills so that it can continue rolling plate for the pipe line required as a matter of urgency to distribute the production of the Alberta Leduc oil wells.
That is the function of the steel controller.
I do not know of anyone who has been subject to the control who would have it otherwise.

There is no doubt that it individual programs were able to shop around among the different producers, and there were no government co-ordinator, certain programs would be well supplied while other programs would be badly upset. I do not know of any producer of steel or pig iron or steel products who would like to see steel control abandoned. I certainly do not know of any user of steel in an important program who would gladly see steel control abandoned.
It has interested me very much to hear our friends say that they are for or against these controls. Apparently the attitude is: "Me too, but the method must be different."
I remember it was said that the Dewey campaign was conducted with the motto, "Me too, but not so much." I think, "Me too; but the method is wrong" accurately describes the Tory position on these matters. In taking that view I think they are overlooking the well-being of the steel industry and of those industries that depend upon steel for their existence.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT. 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Would the minister agree, as to the feeling of satisfaction which he describes, and which I am very much afraid exists in many quarters- there is satisfaction on the part of those who are well established in business, who are content to have business remain as is, who want no one else allowed to come-it is those people who are as content as the minister indicates? If so, I should like to point out that that situation is most injurious to anyone who really believes in the free system.
I am very much afraid that the minister is right in saying that there are a lot of people who like to come down to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that the whole problem that has arisen here in the discussion that is now taking place on the one hand is the direct result of the course that is being followed, and on the other hand indicates the highly unsatisfactory nature of that course. What comes before the committee is a short bill of two sections. The first section of the bill contains a provision that would extend the period of application of these twelve orders in council for another year. The second section refers to the powers of the wartime prices and trade board in connection with these regulations. But obviously the second section dealing with the restriction of the powers of the wartime prices and trade board is something of such a specific nature that it certainly would not be the place where the general or detailed effect of these twelve orders in council could be considered. Therefore unless they can be considered in detail in relation to section 1, there is no place in the whole course of the discussion where they can be considered in detail.
All that is before the house on first reading where there is no debate, on second reading where there is debate on the principle, and ultimately on third reading, is this bill of two sections, the first section carrying forward for another year these twelve orders in council in their entirety. The principle involved in the discussion on second reading was whether or not, in the opinion of this house, the circumstances were such that these twelve orders in council should be continued. If there is any point at which some reasonable limitation might have been placed upon the amount of detail, I think it would be at the time that clear principle was in issue.
Now when we come into committee, in the ordinary course of events there would be before us a bill including in express detail in succeeding sections those things that the government will have power to deal with by an act ultimately adopted by the parliament of Canada. But through the fact that these are not statutory provisions in the ordinary acceptance of that term, but are in fact wartime orders in council carried forward by an all-embracing act of this nature, then unless at this point in committee there is an opportunity to discuss in detail the effect of the provisions of these orders in council carried forward, there is no point during the whole course of the proceedings, from first reading to third reading, where there would be any

Transitional Measures Act opportunity to point out in detail exactly what the result is or to obtain from the ministers concerned an appropriate explanation of what their reasons are for continuing these particular powers or what the effect of the continuance of these particular powers would be.
I close my remarks-only in respect to this discussion that is taking place-by suggesting that the ordinary rules do not apply; because the ordinary rules relate to the introduction of bills which confer powers upon parliament and upon the administrative body of parliament, the government; whereas in this case you have the utterly abnormal situation, from the ordinary point of view of parliamentary procedure, of orders in council adopted under the War Measures Act which, in turn, was an act passed under these emergency powers. May I emphasize that point, Mr. Chairman. These were not orders in council adopted under any general powers available to the government and to parliament in the war. These were orders in council passed under the War Measures Act, which act was within the jurisdiction of this parliament only because of an emergency. That act has disappeared, but the orders in council passed under it are carried forward. Therefore the whole proceeding we have is completely abnormal and completely outside of the ordinary concept of the rules. I submit that, unless there is an opportunity to discuss these orders in council in detail at this point, there could be no opportunity at any time.

THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakeroldname: Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.
He said: Mr. Speaker, once again it is my pleasant duty to bring down the annual budget amid conditions of sustained-one might almost say unexcelled-prosperity. Despite the grave uncertainties and the persistent difficulties that beset us in the field of international affairs, we Canadians as a whole have continued throughout the past year to enjoy higher standards of living than ever before. The volume of industrial output for civilian account, in the form of both consumer goods and capital goods, has never been higher. Cash income derived from farm crops, and the value of commercial fish landings in 1948 have also reached figures never before equalled. The output of our mines has increased by nearly one-third during the past three years, and is now running at a rate within two per cent of the wartime peak.
In other words, during the past year the Canadian economy-and by that phrase I mean this community of a million and a half farmers and fishermen, of three million

The Budget-Mr. Abbott industrial workers, and of hundreds of thousands of business, salaried and professional men and women, great and small-during the past year this community of free people has produced a record quantity of consumer goods, and at the same time has produced and installed a huge amount of new and improved capital equipment which promises still greater output in the years immediately ahead.
But what is even more satisfactory is that the energy, industry, skill and equipment which have been put into industry during the past three or four years is now bearing fruit in the form of a greatly increased flow of goods. Most of the serious shortages of goods have been overcome. The post-war world price inflation appears to have run its course. Since the late summer the price indexes have leveled out both here and in the United States -the two countries in which a free price market most nearly exists. In some sectors of the price structure, where the increases had been particularly great, prices have begun to recede to more healthy levels.
Prediction in a world so full of uncertainties must always be hazardous, but there is a wide measure of agreement, both here and abroad, that, barring the three major catastrophes of war, crop failure and widespread industrial work stoppages, the post-war price inflation has come to an end. That is not to say that there are not some acute shortages, as in steel or in housing, nor that there may not be considerable ups and downs in the prices of individual commodities from week to week and month to month. But the general assumption which I feel justified in making at this point is that when we come to the end of this year and look back we shall find that the price level as a whole will be no higher than it is now and that the prices of some groups of commodities at least will be somewhat lower.
The conditions and prospects which I have thus briefly sketched enable me to recommend to this house a series of proposals which combine a prudent provision against future uncertainties with a considerable measure of immediate tax reduction.
It seems to me that the time has now come when our objective should be to sustain our present high levels of output, avoiding the evils of unemployment on the one hand and further inflation on the other. The aim of both public and private economic policy should be to hold steady on the course. It cannot be the steadiness of inaction. To hold a steady course we must continue to devote much of our effort to further development and betterment. We should not seek just a balance, but a balance in motion.
Of course, we have our pessimists here and elsewhere. There are those whose eyes,
TMr. Abbott.]
fixed firmly on the past, see only the depressions that have followed the booms. But the best opinion I have been able to form leads me to believe that we can hold the current levels if we, and others in like position, act sensibly. I do not expect in the near future any serious decline in the high level of expenditures in North America, upon which our present prosperity is based. Businessmen, public authorities and consumers still have large demands to be filled, and the wherewithal to pay for what they want. Overseas countries still have many requirements to be met from north American production. Their own ability to pay is increasing and in the meantime is being supplemented by assistance from this side of the Atlantic. As I have said, no one can look far into the future with complete assurance in this uncertain age, but we can see far enough to make it possible to lay our plans now in the expectation that something like the present level of production and income for the country as a whole will persist throughout this coming year.
At the time of the last budget our most urgent and difficult economic problem was our shortage of foreign exchange. The progress made in this matter has been evident in our improved trade figures and in the recovery of our exchange reserve.
The present size of our exchange reserves shows the great improvement that has taken place since the end of 1947, when the emergency measures designed first to stop and then to reverse the serious drain on our reserves went into effect. From the dangerously low level of $502 million on December 31, 1947, our reserves rose to $998 million on December 31, 1948, and are now about $1,065 million, a level which, though not yet satisfactory, is much more nearly adequate to safeguard our position against the deficits which could develop without much warning in a trade as large and vulnerable as ours. In appraising this higher figure, one must bear in mind that it includes government borrowing of $150 million in the United States. On the other hand it also reflects the net foreign lending by the government amounting to about $100 million in this 15-month period.
All things considered, the change in our reserve position has been quite remarkable. During most of 1947 we were losing reserves at an average rate of $70 million a month. Since the beginning of 1948, excluding the long-term loan, we have been rebuilding our reserves at an average rate of about $30 million a month. In other words there has been a reversal of trend of the order of about $100 million a month. Improved tourist revenues as well as other invisible items on both cur-

rent and capital account have contributed to this result, but it is clear that the principal increase in our reserves has come through the improvement in our merchandise balance of trade, and in particular our balance with the United States.
The trade figures for the year 1948 as a whole, when compared with 1947, show in a striking way this principal reason for the improvement in our exchange position. Our total exports increased from about $2 [DOT] 8 billion to about $3-1 billion. Most of this increase was due to the higher prices at which our goods were sold, but in some groups of commodities there were satisfactory increases in volume. The total value of our imports remained almost unchanged at about $2-6 billion, despite an average increase in their prices of over 10 per cent. There was therefore an appreciable decrease in the actual volume of goods imported. Taking tourist business, freights, interest and dividends and other similar transactions into account, our net balance on current account transactions with all countries increased from a surplus of only $47 million in 1947 to one of about $450 million in 1948. Hon. members will realize, of course, that in 1948 we were not selling so much on credit and that this larger current balance was not offset to the same extent as in 1947 by large-scale foreign lending.
This improvement in our trade balance took place almost entirely in our trade with the United States. Our exports to Britain and its sterling area were reduced in total value by $130 million, or about 12 per cent, due mainly, of course, to their need to save dollars. Our exports to other countries-mainly European-were reduced by $30 million, or about 5 per cent, for similar reasons. Our imports from both these areas were increased substantially-by $230 million, or nearly 40 per cent. This improvement in the capacity of these areas to resume their pre-war share in supplying our needs has been most welcome. It reflects a fundamental improvement in their productivity and output, as well as their efforts to sell, and our efforts to encourage the resumption of something approaching the pre-war pattern of trade.
On the other hand, our 1948 imports from the United States were $170 million less than in 1947, or a reduction of about 10 per cent, and this despite some sharp increases in the cost of American goods. The reduction of $170 million is the net result of two contrasting trends. In the case of goods enumerated in the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act, the value of imports from the United States was reduced by $300 million; but the volume of all other imports rose by $130
The Budget-Mr. Abbott million. Increases in oil, coal and farm machinery alone amounted to more than $120 million.
But the feature of our trade which I find most encouraging has been the increase in our exports to the United States. Here, the total value increased from just over one billion dollars in 1947 to more than one and a half billions in 1948. Some of this increase is due, of course, to higher prices-especially for pulp and paper and metals. Some of it is due to very large exports of cattle. But much of it, I am glad to say, is the result of improved Canadian ability to produce for, and sell to, the United States market, and of the reductions in tariffs obtained in the Geneva agreements. This big improvement in our exports to the United States was the type of constructive solution to our exchange difficulties that we were hoping to achieve, and I am gratified-as I hope you, sir, and all other hon. members are as well-at the extent of our success in this direction.
To summarize these trade figures briefly, our debit balance with the United States has been reduced by $635 million, and our credit balance with all other countries has gone down by $400 million, leaving a net increase in our over-all credit balance of $235 million.
Our exchange problem is now approaching manageable proportions. As this house is aware from the discussions of the past few days, it is necessary to continue controls over imports as well as capital exchange transactions, in order to improve and safeguard our exchange situation, but these need not be so general or severe as to interfere seriously with the free working of our economy. I shall be announcing later in this statement some further welcome relaxations in these import restrictions, effective April 1.
I cannot leave this discussion of our exchange situation without expressing appreciation of the farsighted actions of the United States in promoting the economic recovery of western Europe. This sensible and practical program has already overcome some of the difficulties which eighteen months ago seemed almost insuperable. It is slowly but surely putting back on its feet one of the great productive areas of the world. This economic restoration is clearly a prerequisite for a stable and progressive political life in this key area, and as such it is a matter vital not only to our future economic well-being but to our very national safety. To us in Canada the general and longer-run benefits of European recovery and progress are of prime importance.	.
The grants and loans being financed through ECA are of great immediate value, but in another and more fundamental way

The Budget-Mr. Abbott the European recovery program is contributing to a betterment of our trading and income prospects. As a result of ERP, and more generally of the broad basic policy which underlies both ERP and the North Atlantic treaty, Europe is rapidly recovering confidence in its own future. The immediate crisis of confidence which was so alarming two years ago has passed. Without this restoration of confidence the large programs of financial aid would have proved merely palliative. As it is, the level of industrial production in western Europe, and for this purpose I include the German bizone, during the last quarter of 1948 was 20 to 25 per cent above the average of 1947, and most of the individual countries in this group have now reached or passed their pre-war levels of industrial output. Of course, much of this output is still going into the repair of the physical ravages of war, and is therefore not yet available for an improvement of standards of living or to pay for the additional imports which the restoration of a normal and rising standard of living demands. The future holds many uncertainties, but we can express gratification for the progress that the first year of ERP has witnessed.
There is one aspect, both of this exchange situation and our own general economic situation, which is clearly going to require continued attention from the government and parliament, as well as from Canadian businessmen. That is the problem of maintaining and extending Canada's overseas exports. In many traditional areas these have been declining during the past year under pressure of their dollar shortage, the adoption or tightening , of import restrictions, and the increased supplies becoming available from other countries. In the light of all these adverse conditions, our export trade has stood up relatively well, but we cannot be satisfied with its present situation or immediate prospects. We must seek improvement. We must search for those adjustments from day to day and month to month that will maintain as far as possible our traditional markets. It was for the purpose of re-establishing and maintaining these traditional markets that we undertook a large export credits program. To the extent that those markets are closed to us, we must develop alternative outlets. While attempting to overcome the immediate difficulties, we must persevere in working out the constructive solution through trade agreements on a wide, non-discriminatory basis, and by other measures of a basic character that will assist those countries that buy from us to find dollar markets for their own exports, in order that they may pay for what they would


really like to get from us. Over the long run, the establishment of prosperous trading conditions must come largely through the reconstruction of those countries overseas with whom we trade, through the expansion of their output and through the recovery of their productive efficiency, so that once again they will be able to earn enough to pay for the imports which they need.
It is only natural in the face of this problem that some should urge us to reverse our basic trade policy and embark upon barter deals, discrimination, and the balancing of trade accounts with individual countries. These are courses that many others are following. Discriminatory deals between others are interfering with our trade. It is tempting in the short run to consider doing similar deals, particularly to sell this or that, where our exports have been supplanted by others. However, it is too easy to look at only one side of the picture. If you look at the country as a whole, if you examine all aspects of the problem, I believe you will find that such a course would not serve Canada's best interests.
We believe that the inevitable effect of these bilateral, discriminatory deals is to diminish the total volume of world trade. However, even apart from this basic objection on grounds of principle, there are also, from Canada's standpoint, serious practical objections. In the first place, most of our trade takes place with the United States-both export and import-and we cannot deal that way there. There is a real danger that we may prejudice this greater part by trying discrimination and barter in the lesser. Secondly, we are not in a good bargaining position to make successful bilateral deals, deals which by their very nature would force us into bilateral balancing with each individual country. The normal and healthy pattern of our trade is triangular or multilateral. We might succeed in selling some surplus products by special deals-but we would have to take some other surpluses in return which we do not want and cannot really use; and for things we want we would be pressed into paying prices which our consumers would be unwilling to pay. In general, the advantage lies with the larger countries in these deals, particularly as sellers' markets give way to buyers' markets. If anyone feels tempted to start this kind of trading in a few problem cases, let him consider how we are likely to get along in the bargaining as we get drawn further and further into it.
The third practical objection to this line of approach is one in which most, but not all, members of this house will agree. It is that the application of a policy of barter, bilateral

deals, and discrimination requires widespread governmental control of private trade, and even the extension of trade by agencies of the government itself. Deals of this sort would require a multiplication of import controls, export controls, licences and permits. It is apt to lead to more government buying and selling, frequently involving subsidies and trading losses. This may fit into the philosophy of government prevailing in some other countries, but most Canadian don't like controls and don't want their government getting deeper and deeper into import and export business.
It is unnecessary, I believe, for me to go into any more detailed review of the economic situation, save such as may be relevant to the appreciation of our fiscal position and policy. As usual I am tabling a white paper that contains, in addition to the detailed estimates of revenue and expenditures for the year now closing, a review of the more important economic statistics for the past few years and recent months. There are also some paragraphs of exposition and comment prepared at my direction and which I commend to those who wish to consider the budget proposals against an economic background. Members of the house and others will recall as well the two recent reports by the governor of the Bank of Canada and the chairman of the foreign exchange control board in which he deals in his usual lucid and objective fashion with the current developments of importance in this field. Finally I should mention the informative facts and forecasts provided some weeks ago to the house by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce, relating particularly to the prospects for capital expenditure and the supplies available for construction.
Several conclusions emerge from an examination of these facts and forecasts. The first is that the prospective amount of capital expenditure on construction and on machinery and equipment, taken together with the level of exports, appears likely to be sufficient to sustain incomes and employment this year at around their current levels. Although the supply of construction materials will be better this year, construction costs are still abnormally high and there is still evidence of some strain upon the industry. I continue to believe that all construction work under the control of the government which it is practicable to postpone should be postponed, except in those few areas where there may be some local unemployment. That has been the approach of the government in the formulation of its expenditure program for the year. I must say that it gets progressively more difficult to apply this policy from year to year, as really important requirements for
The Budget-Mr. Abbott construction of all kinds keep accumulating -some of them repeatedly deferred since long before the war. Other needs, too, are constantly arising-some of them from the necessary expansion in the defence program, others from more constructive developments, such as the need to provide improved airport runways and related equipment to accommodate the bigger and better planes now available. We have also given a fairly high priority to construction necessary to permit expansion in our government activities in the field of scientific research and the improvement of techniques and markets for primary production-government operations which we feel are as fruitful as much private work with which they must compete for materials and labour. I hope this view will commend itself to the house and the public.
A second conclusion that emerges from a review of the economic situation is that the pressure of consumer expenditures upon supplies available to consumers is slackening. This may be observed in respect of various particular commodities where consumers can get what they want more easily and promptly than before, even motor cars. In some cases we can observe the occasional emergence of surpluses and of bargain sales by retailers, something which we had almost forgotten to be a normal part of business at certain seasons of the year.
This improvement in the supply situation for consumer goods results mainly from an increase in their supply and, to a lesser extent, I believe, from the filling up of the more urgent needs of consumers deferred during the war and the post-war shortages. Larger supplies of food have resulted from good crops here and elsewhere last year, both in the United States and abroad. The post-war world food shortage is passing over from its acute stage to a less severe phase in which prices and the ability to pay them are governing considerations once more. In other types of goods we are beginning now to receive the increased output in Canada made possible by our extended and improved equipment installed in recent years, as well as the increased imports from overseas as a result of the recovery of production in Europe and elsewhere, and the efforts of various countries to export to our markets.
This improvement in consumer supplies has brought a welcome halt to the increase in the cost of living. The index of living costs has remained almost constant since last September at a level about 60 per cent above pre-war, and about 30 per cent above 1929. Decreases in food costs have offset slight increases in other items. Some further increases may occur in a few items; but I think we are unlikely to see any significant

The Budget-Mr. Abbott increase in the cost of living this year- unless, of course, there are serious crop failures-and it is quite possible that there may be some decline. Consumers should have more money to spend this year than last, partly because of the upward sweep in wages that took place last year, partly because of the distribution of wartime refundable taxes that has been going on this month, partly because of additional payments being made to farmers by the wheat board, and partly as a result of the tax reductions which I shall be inviting this house to approve. The time has now come, I believe, when these increased expenditures by consumers can be met by increased supplies of goods without endangering either our price structure or our exchange situation.
In the light of these conditions and in line with the policy to which we have steadily adhered of removing controls at the earliest appropriate time, the government has authorized the wartime prices and trade board to withdraw its price ceiling orders on flour, bread, butter, sugar and molasses, and on those fruits and vegetables which are not limited in supply by the operation of the present import restrictions. Concurrently the government is withdrawing the subsidy of 46J cents a bushel which has been paid since August 1 last on wheat going into domestic consumption in Canada.
Before turning to a review of the government accounts for the year, I wish to say a few words in regard to provincial matters.
We are now about to enter the third of the five fiscal years covered by our tax rental agreements with seven of the provinces. Those agreements have enabled the provinces concerned to obtain a more equitable share of revenue from the three great sources of direct taxation. They have done so without subjecting the taxpayers of these provinces to dual assessments, dual reporting and the other inconveniences and vexations which double taxation involves. They have enabled all these provinces to have the revenue from these major sources reflect the growth of population and the expansion of national income, and at the same time to have the assurance of an underwriting against the risks of economic adversity. This assurance that, come what may, cash receipts from these important tax sources could not fall below a guaranteed minimum has been, I believe, of great importance in enabling provincial governments to plan in advance their developmental programs and to undertake them with confidence. It has certainly also improved the credit standing of the provinces concerned. From the national point of view, it has removed or vastly lessened the risk that in


times of economic difficulty the financial strains to which some provincial governments would be subject might lead to a competitive scramble to impose new and higher taxes and to adopt other policies which would hamper and impede national policies designed to promote economic recovery. They have provided a partial, though not yet a complete, basis for the development of that comprehensive program of co-operation between the federal and the provincial governments which we envisaged as essential to promote the maximum development of our resources and to assure full employment and a wide measure of social security for the Canadian people as a whole.
In all these ways the agreements have contributed to the strength and independence of provincial governments and to the health and vitality of the Canadian confederation. They have added a large measure of economic autonomy to the political autonomy enjoyed by the provinces which have entered into them. It is a travesty to suggest, as has been done so many times in this house in recent weeks, that they have weakened provincial autonomy or created an undue degree of centralization in this country. Two attempts have been made to build a case to support this charge.
The first attempt was based on the argument that the tax rental agreements involved an excessive use of subsidies which threatened the freedom of action of the provincial governments. In reply to that it should first be pointed out that the payments being made to the provinces under the tax rental agreements, apart from the statutory subsidies, are not subsidies at all; they are rentals negotiated by provincial governments for the temporary use of certain rights possessed by them. They are business-like arrangements, subject to re-negotiation at least a year before their termination date, and they do not involve the element of charity nor the surrender of one jot or tittle of constitutional rights. In most of these respects they are in marked contrast with the alternative which some of the critics suggest, namely, fiscal need subsidies which would require the provincial governments to come hat in hand to the federal government and plead for assistance on the basis of need rather than of right.
That should be a sufficient answer to the argument. However, even if we take both the tax rentals and statutory subsidies, we find that the total payments being made by the federal government to the provinces constitute a lower percentage of provincial ordinary revenues than the percentage of statutory subsidies to total ordinary revenues

in the case of the four original provinces during the first fifteen years after they joined together to form our confederation. Let me give the figures. In the fifteen fiscal years 1868-1882, Nova Scotia derived 74-1 per cent of its ordinary revenue from federal subsidies; in the current fiscal year it is estimated that only 36-1 per cent of its ordinary revenue will come from subsidies and tax rental agreement payments. The corresponding figures in the case of New Brunswick are 77-9 per cent for the earlier period and an estimated 36-9 per cent for the current year. In the first fifteen years after confederation, Ontario derived 39-9 per cent of its total ordinary revenue from federal subsidies and Quebec 45-1 per cent; if these provinces were participating under the agreement, the percentage of their ordinary revenue derived from tax rentals and subsidies would, it is estimated, be moderately lower than the percentages I have just quoted. In the years following confederation up to 1882, all provinces, on the average, obtained 49-8 per cent of their total ordinary revenues from federal subsidies. For all seven provinces which enjoy the benefits of the tax rental agreement, the percentage of total ordinary revenues derived from tax rentals and subsidies in the current fiscal year is now estimated at only 32 per cent. If such percentages be the test, it is amply clear that we have far less centralization and make much less use of subsidies than the fathers of confederation thought to be necessary and provided for in the making of Canada.
The second attempt was based on the argument that between 1939 and 1947 the increase in dominion tax revenues had been much greater than in the case of the provincial and municipal governments. The simple answer to that argument, of course, is that during the period in question Canada has fought a major war involving the federal government in a perfectly colossal cost and leaving behind it an enormous burden in debt charges, pensions, treatment service costs, rehabilitation and other expenditures for which this government will be responsible for many years to come-and so will it also be for the vastly increased national defence expenditures which the state of the world left by that war is making it necessary for us to carry.
Neither of these arguments stands up nor do any of a similar kind. The simple fact is that the tax rental agreements promote and encourage provincial autonomy by making the provincial governments better able to carry out the heavy responsibilities assigned to them by our constitution. This government yields to no one in its desire to protect their rights and see them financially strong and independent. It yields to no one in its 29087-113
The Budget-Mr. Abbott desire to co-operate with them in that kind of constructive partnership which will best enable all governments to tackle and solve the complicated problems of today and give to the Canadian people the measure of peace, prosperity and happiness they have a right to expect.
In this search for co-operation, it will not let pettiness of spirit nor false pride nor undue emphasis on purely financial considerations stand in the way of mutual understanding and constructive results. It will constantly seek out ways of tackling mutual problems and developing practical solutions. -not merely talking about them as some other people do.
THE GOVERNMENT ACCOUNTS: REVIEW OP 1948-49 AND FORECAST FOR 1949-50
Before appraising the budgetary outlook for the coming fiscal year, it is my duty to report to the house the financial results of the year that is now drawing to its close. The white paper which I am tabling includes the usual detailed statements of revenues and expenditures, and of assets and liabilities. The figures for the year 1948-49 are necessarily preliminary and subject to revision. Our fiscal year ends next week, on March 31, but our books must remain open for several weeks thereafter to record various year-end adjustments and to include all payments made up to April 30 on account of expenditures originating in, and properly chargeable to, the current fiscal year. Final figures for this current year cannot be available for some time.
A year ago I forecast revenue and expenditure figures that would yield a surplus of $489 million. The present figures indicate that our revenues will be $2,768 million, our expenditures $2,193 million, and our surplus $575 million. This surplus of $575 million is $100 million less than we had in the preceding year, but it is $86 million greater than I had forecast for this current year.
A year ago I based my estimates on what I then called a "conservatively optimistic forecast." In fact the expansion of the national income has been somewhat greater than that which I had predicted, and as a result our tax revenues are turning out a little better than the forecast, but the excess is not very great-less than 2\ per cent. We will obtain more from non-tax revenues and special receipts and credits than I had forecast, but expenditures, on the other hand, are within 1 per cent of my forecast.

I do not propose to comment at length on the details of revenue and expenditure, but shall content myself, and I hope the house, with a few general remarks.
Direct taxes, which include personal and corporate income taxes, the excess profits tax and succession duties have yielded $1,369 million, or $51 million greater than a year ago. They accounted for more than 56 per cent of our total tax revenue.
Indirect taxes, which include all customs and excise taxes and duties, have produced $ls172 million, or $62 million less than a year ago.
The greater yield in direct taxes is a reflection of higher incomes and profits; the decrease in indirect taxes is the result of the lower rates of duty under the Geneva agreements, the restriction of imports under the Emergency Exchange Conservation Act and the removal a year ago of the amusement tax, the sales taxes on prepared and packaged foods, and certain other indirect taxes.
Non-tax revenues, that is, post-office receipts and revenues from investments, were $210 million, or $32 million greater than last year. Special receipts and credits, chiefly sales of surplus war assets and sundry refunds, amounted to $117 million. This is $125 million less than a year ago.
On the expenditure side the principal decrease is $229 million in demobilization, reconversion and special expenditures. This decrease was almost exactly balanced by increases of $203 million in ordinary expenditures and $21 million in the deficits of government owned enterprises.
To a considerable extent this increase in ordinary expenditures is due to transfers of activities from the demobilization accounts to the ordinary accounts, and for the rest it stems from higher old age pensions, increased numbers of persons entitled to family allowances, the expansion of health services, more exploration, survey and mapping work, increased research expenditures, improved roads and tourist facilities in our national parks, improvements in airports and aids to air navigation, the betterment of maritime ports

and harbours works, and generally from the effects of the higher price levels of all government operations, including the costs of construction and the costs of materials and supplies purchased, and including necessary adjustments in civil service salaries. I am very keenly aware of these increases in expenditures, and I can assure the house that we are constantly striving to maintain and improve both efficiency and economy in all government activities.
In summary then, our revenues for the year now ending are $103 million less than the preceding year, expenditures as a whole are down $2 million, and the surplus of $575 million is $101 million less than last year. There, in brief, is the result of our current financial operations for the year, and that is the amount by which the net debt of Canada has been reduced.
But, as has to be pointed out each year, the cash position and the cash requirements of the government, as distinct from its revenues and expenditures, are of almost equal importance in their bearing upon the incomes and expenditures of the individuals who make up this nation. Apart entirely from the sale of new securities or the redemption of old debt, the government receives and pays out each year large sums of cash that do not really belong to what an accountant might call its "income account",-they are neither revenue nor expenditure in the accounting or budgetary sense. Moreover some items of revenue and expenditure do not involve any cash receipts or cash outlays.
To arrive at our cash surplus, the $575 million budget surplus must be adjusted upward by $75 million on account of these non-cash items. Then we must add $128 million of cash receipts in the form of additions to various pension and trust accounts. This gives us a total of $778 million available for cash outlays that do not belong in the income account. The greater part of the reduction in the funded debt has taken the form of repaying approximately $286 million on account of the compulsory savings portion of the personal income taxes of 1943 and 1944, and the refundable portion of the excess profits taxes of 1943. This completes the repayment of the refundable portion of personal income taxes.
I must not leave this part of my report to the house without referring to the very gratifying response to our offerings of Canada savings bonds to the general public. As hon. members know, the purchase of these bonds is restricted to individuals and is limited to not more than $1,000 of any one series to any one person. Sales of the second series of these bonds reached $288 million. A third series was opened for subscription last October, and sales to date are $248 million. The public response to these issues, and particularly the volume of subscriptions made through the payroll savings plan, shows that Canada savings bonds fill very acceptably a real investment need for the rank and file of the Canadian people.
These results for the year should be a source of gratification to all Canadians. We have reduced our net debt by $575 million at the time when we could best afford to do so. It is still a very large debt-a net debt of $11-8 billion, and a total funded debt of $15-6 billion. There will undoubtedly be years when we will need to increase it in order to finance expenditures in excess of revenue, when economic conditions make that wise or necessary. An indefinite growth in the debt, and in the cost of servicing it, must eventually undermine confidence in our currency and our national finances.
I think most Canadians will regard the policy we have followed as one of simple common sense. Yet some hon. members opposite have insisted that we should have been less prudent, that we should not have attempted to reduce our debt this year, that we should have borrowed to pay off refundable savings or to finance the recovery in our exchange reserves. While arguing that taxes should have been drastically lower, they have also been urging higher and higher expenditures on a bewildering variety of projects. I ask myself how anyone can take as serious and responsible criticisms of this kind. They ask us to believe that the people of Canada would have been better off this past year had taxes been substantially lower, and our debt substantially higher.
That is not the case. Large tax reductions last year would have come too early to be of real value to the public as a whole.
